items.stem: Which data firm harvested data from up to 87 million Facebook users for political campaigning, as revealed in 2018?
items.answer: Cambridge Analytica
items.markingKey: D. Facebook was fined $5 billion by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019.

items.stem: Explain why technology companies are considered powerful political actors.
items.answer: Platforms control information flows for billions, set rules on speech through content moderation, collect vast data, and can resist or comply with state demands, giving them structural power beyond many states.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Platforms control information flows for billions, set rules on speech through content moderation, collect vast data, and can resist or comply with state demands, giving them structural power beyond many states. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Chloé writes: "Only authoritarian states engage in mass surveillance." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Democracies also conduct mass surveillance, as Edward Snowden’s 2013 revelations about US and UK programmes showed.
items.markingKey: Democracies also conduct mass surveillance, as Edward Snowden’s 2013 revelations about US and UK programmes showed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Kenyan Finance Bill protests (2024) and explain what it reveals about social media and political mobilisation.
items.answer: Young Kenyans used TikTok, X and crowdfunding to organise protests against tax rises; the President withdrew the bill, though dozens of protesters were killed. Digital tools enabled rapid, leaderless mobilisation that forced a policy reversal, while state repression showed the limits of online power.
items.markingKey: Context (Young Kenyans used TikTok, X and crowdfunding to organise protests against tax rises; the President withdrew the bill, though dozens of protesters were killed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Digital tools enabled rapid, leaderless mobilisation that forced a policy reversal, while state repression showed the limits of online power. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to social media and political mobilisation.

items.answer: Social media makes mobilisation faster and larger, but not necessarily more effective in achieving lasting change.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "disinformation"?
options: False or misleading information deliberately created and spread to deceive, often for political purposes
An approach, used by the EU AI Act (2024), that sets stricter rules for AI applications according to the risk they pose, banning those with “unacceptable” risk
Shared digital systems such as digital identity, payments and data exchange, provided as public goods, e.g. India’s Aadhaar and UPI

items.stem: Explain the difference between state surveillance and surveillance capitalism.
items.answer: State surveillance is monitoring by governments for security or control; surveillance capitalism is the collection of personal data by private companies to predict and shape behaviour for profit.
items.markingKey: State surveillance is monitoring by governments for security or control; surveillance capitalism is the collection of personal data by private companies to predict and shape behaviour for profit. items.stem: Briefly explain why leaderless digital movements may struggle to achieve long-term change.
items.answer: Rapid online mobilisation can bypass organisation-building; without leaders, programmes and negotiating structures, movements may fragment after initial success, as Zeynep Tufekci argued in Twitter and Tear Gas (2017).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the EU is described as a regulatory superpower in technology.
items.answer: Its large market means firms adopt EU standards globally to avoid separate systems (the “Brussels effect”), so laws such as the GDPR and AI Act influence practices worldwide.

items.answer: It involves political choices about rights, power, competition and security, and is contested between states, firms and civil society.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Data sovereignty protects citizens more than it empowers governments."
items.answer: Its effects depend on regime type: it protects citizens under rights-based laws but empowers governments in authoritarian states.

items.answer: The multistakeholder model involves states, companies, technical bodies and civil society (e.g. ICANN), favoured by Western states; the multilateral model gives states primary control through intergovernmental bodies, favoured by China and Russia.

items.answer: Access to the internet affects education, jobs, health services and political participation; unequal access reinforces existing inequalities and depends on public investment and regulation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Technology transfer from the Global North has created dependence rather than development."
items.answer: Transfer can foster dependence, but its development impact depends on local capacity and the terms of transfer.

items.stem: Explain why technology transfer to developing countries is contested.
items.answer: Developing states seek access to technologies (e.g. for climate mitigation or vaccines), while firms and states in the Global North protect intellectual property and competitive advantage.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the access divide and the skills (usage) divide.
items.answer: The access divide concerns whether people have devices and connectivity; the skills divide concerns whether they can use technology effectively, which persists even when access improves.

items.answer: Lance Bennett and Alexandra Segerberg’s term for mobilisation organised through personalised sharing on digital networks rather than through formal organisations

items.answer: About 2.6 billion

items.stem: Explain the difference between voluntary AI principles and binding regulation of AI.
items.answer: Binding regulation creates legal obligations and penalties (EU AI Act); voluntary principles rely on commitments by states or firms (OECD AI Principles, Bletchley Declaration).

items.stem: Distinguish between cyber-pessimism and cyber-optimism.
items.answer: Cyber-optimists (e.g. Clay Shirky) see digital technology as empowering citizens and spreading democracy; cyber-pessimists (e.g. Evgeny Morozov) stress its use for surveillance, censorship and manipulation.

items.stem: Explain why lethal autonomous weapons raise ethical and legal concerns.
items.answer: Delegating life-and-death decisions to machines raises questions about compliance with international humanitarian law (distinction, proportionality), accountability for errors, and lowering the threshold for war.

items.stem: Using US export controls on advanced semiconductors (from 2022) as an example, explain technology as a domain of great-power competition.
items.answer: The USA restricted exports of advanced AI chips and chip-making equipment to China, citing national security; China responded with controls on critical minerals such as gallium and germanium. Control over key technologies became a tool of geopolitical rivalry, linking technology governance to security.
